title: Sanctions against Nicholas Bowerman for failure to co-operate with an investigation by the Financial Reporting Council
text:
The FRC has published the report of the Disciplinary Tribunal (the Tribunal) appointed
under paragraph 9(2) of the Accountancy Scheme to hear the Formal Complaint brought by
the FRC’s Executive Counsel against Nicholas Bowerman relating to his conduct in failing to
comply with his duty to co-operate with an investigation by the FRC’s Executive Counsel.
The sole purpose of the Tribunal was to hear and determine the Formal Complaint made
against Mr Bowerman and brought by the FRC’s Executive Counsel, and to do so on the
basis of the evidence and arguments relied upon by those parties.
The Tribunal Report follows a public hearing. The Tribunal has not made, and should not be
taken to have made, any finding against any persons or entities other than Mr Bowerman. It
would not be fair to treat any part of the Tribunal’s findings, including any part(s) of the
Tribunal Report, as constituting or evidencing findings against anyone other than Mr
Bowerman.
The published Tribunal Report has been edited for publication and anonymises several third
parties, who are instead identified by various descriptors and ciphers.

In the matter of:
The Executive Counsel to the Financial Reporting Council
- and -
Nicholas Bowerman

Decision of the Disciplinary Tribunal

Mr James Potts, represented the Executive Counsel to the FRC.
There was no appearance by or on behalf of Nicholas Bowerman.

Introduction
1.
This is the Decision of the Disciplinary Tribunal (‘the Tribunal’), consisting of The
Hon. Lady Wolffe (Chair), Mark Williams (Accountant Member) and Manu Duggal
(Lay Member) appointed by the Convener under paragraphs 9(2) and 11(2) of the

2
Accountancy Scheme (‘the Scheme’)1 to hear the Formal Complaint2 initiated by the
Executive Counsel to the Financial Reporting Council (‘FRC’) in respect of Mr
Nicholas Bowerman (the ‘Respondent’). While the members of Tribunal concurred on
the outcome and on the issue of sanction, Mr Duggal preferred to provide his own
reasons on several aspects concerning sanction and costs, and which are provided in his
separate Note of Reasons.

2.
The Respondent is a member of the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants
‘CIMA’), a professional body which is a Participant in the Scheme and, as such, he is a
’Member’ for the purposes of the Scheme.

Pipeline Engineering & Supply Co Ltd
3.
The Respondent was formerly the Finance Director of Pipeline Engineering & Supply
Co Ltd (“Pipeline”), now in voluntary liquidation. Pipeline was a UK subsidiary of a
US listed company, [Company X].

[Company X]’s SEC public filing; the [Company X] Report
4.
In March 2022, [Company X] made a public filing to the United States Securities and
Exchange Commission (‘the SEC’) that [Company X] had uncovered accounting
irregularities at Pipeline…[redacted]. 3

5.
[Company X] instructed American forensic accountants to review and analyse the
financial data for Pipeline and [Company X] for a five-year period, to review internal
documentation and to conduct interviews for the purposes of producing a report (‘the
[Company X] Report’)4 into these irregularities. [Redacted].

1 The Accountancy Scheme has effect from 1 January 2021 and was reissued on 30 March 2021. References in
this Decision to paragraph numbers of the Scheme are to the paragraph numbers in the 30 March 2021 reissue.
https://media.frc.org.uk/documents/Accountancy-Scheme-March-21_1.pdf

2 Dated 19 December 2024 and produced in the Hearing Bundle (‘HB’) at p18ff. Documents in the HB will be
identified in this decision by their description and page number in the HB.

3 [Redacted].

4 HB p 71ff.

3

4
FRC Investigation resulting in the Formal Complaint
6.
On 20 June 2023, the Conduct Committee of the FRC decided to institute an
investigation under the Scheme into the conduct of the Respondent in his role as the
Finance Director of Pipeline. The scope of that investigation related to the preparation
and provision of financial information of Pipeline for the financial years ended 31
December 2017 to 31 December 2021 (defined as ‘the Investigation’ in the Formal
Complaint). [The ‘FRC Senior Lawyer’], a Senior Lawyer in the Enforcement Division
of the FRC, took the lead in the Investigation.

7.
The subject matter of the SEC filing and the allegations in the [Company X] Report are
not the subject of the Formal Complaint. Rather, it is the Respondent’s alleged failure
to cooperate in the 12 months or so following the initiation of that Investigation. In due
course, a Proposed Formal Complaint was intimated to the Respondent (on 10
September 2024).

8.
While the evidence relied upon for each of the two allegations will be set out in full
below, it suffices to summarise the alleged breaches of duty incumbent upon the
Respondent under the Scheme, namely, by:

1. Failing to respond to communications from Executive Counsel, in
contravention of paragraph 14(1) of the Scheme. In particular, the Respondent
failed to respond to a number of attempts by Executive Counsel to make
contact with him for the purposes of the Investigation; and
2. Failing to comply with a notice issued by Executive Counsel under paragraph
14(2) of the Scheme (‘the para 14(2) Notice’). In particular, failing to contact
the FRC Lawyer with suggested times for an interview, either by the deadline
of 28 June 2024 or at all.
9.
Given the nature of the allegations, it should be noted that in the course of the
Investigation the FRC had established the current email, home address and phone
number of the Respondent and it is to one or more of these that communications and
documents were sent. The steps taken by the FRC to ascertain these are noted below5.

5 See paragraphs 24 to 30 of [the FRC Senior Lawyer]’s Statement, quoted in paragraph [68], below

5

Formal notifications to the Respondent under the Scheme
i)
Commencement of the Investigation
10. The Conduct Committee of the FRC gave notice to the Respondent on 22 June 2023
under paragraph 7(4)(ii) of the Scheme of the opening of an investigation into his
conduct in relation to the preparation and provision of the financial information of
Pipeline for the financial years ended 31 December 2017 to 31 December 20216. The
authority to give notice is found in paragraph 6(8) of the Scheme and may only be done
if at least one of the two criteria in paragraph 5(1) are met, taking into consideration the
matters in paragraph 5(2) of the Scheme. In this instance, the Conduct Committee was
of the opinion that the matter raised or appeared to raise ‘important issues affecting the
public interest in the UK’ and that there were reasonable grounds to consider there may
have been Misconduct on the part of the Respondent.

ii)
Intimation of Proposed Formal Complaint
11. The next formal step was the intimation to the Respondent of the Proposed Formal
Complaint issued under paragraph 7(10) of the Scheme7, which was sent by email to
the Respondent on 10 September 2024, inviting the Respondent to make written
representations within eight weeks and explaining the next steps under the Scheme. A
reminder to do so was sent on 11 October 20248.

12. About three weeks later, on 29 October 2024, the Respondent emailed [the FRC Senior
Lawyer] as follows: ‘Please confirm this is now complete’. [The FRC Senior Lawyer]
immediately replied, requesting clarification. Shortly thereafter, [the FRC Senior
Lawyer] received an unsigned email asking, ‘Do you now have everything?’.9 Again,
[the FRC Senior Lawyer] replied immediately asking if the Respondent had sent a
response to the Proposed Formal Complaint, indicating that no such response had been
received. There is no record of any reply by the Respondent to either of these emails

6 The same definition of Investigation is used in the Formal Complaint (at paragraph 7).

7 At the same time the means for access to the supporting documentation were also provided: see paragraphs 38
and 39 of the Formal Complaint.

8 See paragraph 40 of the Formal Complaint.

9 These exchanges are recorded in paragraph 21 of the Formal Complaint.

6
from [the FRC Senior Lawyer]. For completeness, it is noted that [the FRC Senior
Lawyer] received a telephone call from the Respondent’s known mobile number, but
the call was disconnected when [the FRC Senior Lawyer] answered10.

13. The Respondent made no written representations (due by 5 November 2024) on the
Proposed Formal Complaint within the deadline, or subsequently. That remained the
position as at the commencement of the Hearing, on 12 May 2025.

iii)
Intimation of intention to initiate the Formal Complaint

14. By letter dated 13 December 2024, intimation was given to the Respondent that the
Executive Counsel would shortly be delivering the Formal Complaint to the Conduct
Committee; that the Conduct Committee would serve the Formal Complaint on the
Respondent and that a Disciplinary Tribunal would be convened to hear the Formal
Complaint11. At the same time, the Respondent’s attention was drawn to the
Accountancy Scheme Sanctions Guidance12 (‘the Sanctions Guidance’), and in
particular to the provisions providing for a discount for any admissions or settlement.

10 See paragraph 42 of the Formal Complaint.

11 HB, p 231.

12 Dated March 2021 and produced at HB, p137ff.

7
Appointment of the Tribunal and Hearing fixed to hear the Formal Complaint
15. In due course a two-day hearing of the Tribunal was fixed, for 12 and 13 May 2025, to
hear the Formal Complaint. The usual directions were made for intimation and
exchange of witness statements, copies of documents, skeleton arguments and
authorities relied upon13. In addition, Executive Counsel was required to provide the
Respondent with copies of any unused material that was in her possession and which
was capable of assisting the Respondent’s case or undermining Executive Counsel's
case, or to confirm to the Tribunal and the Respondent that she did not have any such
material in her possession. By email dated 11 April 2025, the Executive Counsel
provided the confirmation sought. The Respondent did not produce any witness
statement or documents of his own.

16. Executive Counsel indicated that in the event of an Adverse Finding, she would seek a
sanction in the form of a three-to-five-year exclusion of the Respondent.

17. By email dated 2 April 2025 [the FRC Senior Lawyer] wrote on behalf of the Executive
Counsel to remind the Respondent of the Tribunal due to begin on 12 May, and advised
the Respondent that he was entitled to be represented by a legal representative at the
hearing14. He noted that the Respondent had not replied to the FRC’s query at the outset
of the Investigation as to whether the Respondent was legally represented and he
suggested that the Respondent ‘consider the benefits of having legal representation, in
light of the sanctions that can be imposed by a Disciplinary Tribunal’ and which he
noted were set out in Appendix 1 to the Scheme. He provided a hyperlink to the
Scheme15. In that same email, he also noted that if costs were a factor there was
information available online about free sources of legal representation and he provided
a hyperlink to the ‘Getting free legal advice’ webpage for The Law Society.

18. [The FRC Senior Lawyer] also drew the Respondent’s attention to paragraph 17 of the
Scheme, whose terms he set out, and which states:

13 The Executive Counsel was required to provide these to the Respondent and the Disciplinary Tribunal by 11
April, and the Respondent by 25 April.
14 See HB, p 233.

15 https://media.frc.org.uk/documents/Accountancy-Scheme-March-21_1.pdf

8

‘17
If, on the application of a Member, a Tribunal concludes that:-
(i) it is not reasonable to expect a Member to conduct their defence or pursue
their appeal without legal representation because, for example, of the
complexities of the issues involved; and
(ii) the Member has established that they cannot afford (and does not have
adequate insurance cover for) legal representation, the Tribunal may require
the FRC to meet the reasonable costs of that Member’s legal representation at
the hearing before the Tribunal.’

19. There was no reply by the Respondent at that time.

9
Emergence of the Preliminary issue and the Respondent’s other communication on 12
May

(i)
The Respondent’s email of 6 May

20. On Tuesday 6 May 2025, in the week preceding the date fixed for the hearing, the
Respondent emailed the Secretary to the Tribunal, stating:

‘I am unsure what evidence you require from me as I have no access to any files or
reports from Pipeline, and have had none since January 2022. Additionally, I would
like to have representation, but have no means to pay for it. Is there a process for
this?’

21. At the Tribunal’s direction, the Secretary to the Tribunal communicated the following
by email on Wednesday 7 May, namely:
‘Dear Mr Bowerman, [the FRC Senior Lawyer],

Mr Bowerman sent an email to the Secretary to the Tribunal yesterday, 6 May
2025. This email was provided to the Tribunal and is attached below.

The Tribunal has noted the points raised by Mr Bowerman.

There are now three working days before the hearing of this matter is
scheduled to commence. The Tribunal confirms its intention that the hearing
will commence, as scheduled, at 10.00 on Monday 12 May 2025 and
continuing on Tuesday 13 May 2025. The Tribunal's intention is to consider
the points raised by Mr Bowerman in his email as preliminary issues, on the
first morning of the hearing.

Mr Bowerman is asked to confirm whether he intends to attend the
hearing. Mr Bowerman should be aware, as he was previously informed in
the Tribunal Secretary's email of 27 March 2025, that if he does not attend the
hearing, the Tribunal may exercise its discretion to proceed in his absence
and consider the preliminary issues as well as any hearing to follow thereon.

The Tribunal now directs that:
1. Mr Bowerman should confirm whether he intends to be present in
person at the hearing by 17.00 today, Wednesday 7 May 2025;
2. FRC Executive Counsel should provide its preliminary response to
the issues raised in Mr Bowerman's email by 14.00 on Thursday 8
May 2025.’

10
22. [The FRC Senior Lawyer] copied the Respondent into his email providing Executive
Counsel’s response to the Tribunal’s direction on 8 May 2025, which again drew the
Respondent’s attention to paragraph 17 of the Scheme16.
23. There was no response by the Respondent in respect of this issue.

(ii)
The Respondent’s email on 12 May

24. On the morning of the 12 May, shortly before the hearing was due to commence, the
Secretary to the Tribunal received the following email from the Respondent (at 9:38):

‘I am unable to attend today as I have had to take my [family member] to the
hospital.’

25. The Secretary to the Tribunal immediately replied by email and tried to contact the
Respondent by telephone, but without success. At the Tribunal’s request, the Secretary
to the Tribunal communicated with the Respondent in the following terms:

‘Dear Mr Bowerman
The Tribunal has received and considered your email below and has instructed me to
respond to you as follows:
1. The Tribunal will allow you until 2pm today to provide evidence of the
reason for your non-availability today to me.
2. Please be aware that if no communication is received from you by 2pm
today, the Tribunal may decide to proceed to hear the case in your absence.
3. Given the reason you have indicated for your non-availability today, please
indicate on what date you would be available to attend the hearing.
The Tribunal expects a response from you by 2pm as indicated. I am also asked to
convey this message to you by telephone and text message.’

26. The Respondent’s only reply, received at 12:46 pm on that day, was to email the
following message:

‘Appointment reminder with Adult Physiotherapy on 12 May 2025 09:00 at Darlington
Memorial Hospital. For queries phone [redacted].
The above is the text message received.’

16 As he had previously done, on 2 April 2025. See paragraph [18], above.

11

12
The preliminary issue

(i)
The Tribunal’s concern in light of the Respondent’s email of 6 May
27. Pending the Respondent’s reply to the Tribunal’s request for evidence of his non-
availability by reason of an apparent medical appointment for a family member, the
Tribunal convened on the morning of 12 May, notwithstanding the absence of the
Respondent. It did so as it wished to raise a matter potentially arising from the second
sentence of the Respondent’s email of 6 May 2025, which it referred to as ‘the
preliminary issue’, with the Executive Counsel’s counsel, Mr Potts.

28. Without making any factual determination, the Tribunal noted that the second sentence
of the Respondent’s email of 6 May 2025 could support the inferences that the
Respondent wished to contest (at least to some extent) the allegations in the Formal
Complaint or any sanction sought, and for which he desired legal representation. While
Mr Potts relied on the terms of paragraph 17 of the Scheme17 and contended that the
second sentence of the Respondent’s email of 6 May did not constitute an application
under that paragraph, in the Tribunal’s view compliance with the terms of paragraph 17
was not necessarily conclusive so as to ensure respect for the fair trial rights of the
Respondent. The Tribunal itself has a duty to ensure respect for a person’s fair trial
rights under Article 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights (‘ECHR’).

29. The supports or safeguards necessary to ensure the fair trial rights of a person who had
no legal representation differed if the proceedings were civil or if they involved the
‘determination of a criminal charge’ (in a Convention sense). In this context, the
classification of proceedings as civil proceedings under domestic law is not conclusive
of that characterisation (i.e. such as to preclude the application of Article 6(3)) but
requires consideration of the three limbs of the Engel test18. If the proceedings to
address the Formal Complaint involved the ‘determination of a criminal charge’, that

17 Set out at paragraph [18], above.

18 Engel and Others v the Netherlands, 8 June 1976, paragraph 82, Series A no. 22 (‘Engel’). The three criteria
are (i) the legal classification of the offence under national law, (ii) the nature of the offence and (iii) the degree
of severity of the penalty that the person risks incurring (collectively, ‘the Engel test’).

13
raised the question of the Respondent’s entitlement to legal representation as this was
one of the minimum (albeit not absolute) rights contained in Article 6(3)19.

30. The Tribunal noted that there is ample authority to the effect that professional
disciplinary proceedings do not involve the determination of a criminal charge, even if
they involved the imposition of a substantial fine (Brown v United Kingdom20
(‘Brown’)), applied by the majority of the Court in Han and another v Customs and
Excise Commissioners21 (‘Han’)). However, other forms of proceedings, such as the
imposition of penalties as part of the enforcement of competition rules against price-
fixing (SA-Capital OY v Finland22) and the imposition of tax penalties by HMRC for
failure to comply with notices under tax statutes23, had been characterised as involving
the ‘determination of a criminal charge’- thereby bringing into consideration the rights
in Article 6(3) of the ECHR.

31. Moreover, the Tribunal drew Mr Potts’ attention to observations of the ECtHR in the
recent case of SA-Capital OY v Finland (‘SA-Capital OY’) that ‘the autonomous
interpretation adopted by the Convention institutions of the notion of a ‘criminal
charge’ under the so-called Engel criteria has led to a gradual broadening of the scope
of the criminal limb of Article 6 to cases not strictly belonging to the traditional
categories of criminal law’24. The observation in SA-Capital OY was suggestive that the

19 Namely, the right ‘to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has
not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be give it free when the interests of justice so require’ in
Article 6(3)(c).

20 (1998) 28 EHRR CD 233 (‘Brown’). In Ramos Nunes de Carvahlho E SÁ v Portugal (Applications nos.
55391/13, 57728/13 and 74041/13) (‘Ramos’) the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights
(‘ECtHR’) re-affirmed the approach in Brown, at paragraphs [123] to [126] of Ramos: sanctions that were
‘purely disciplinary in nature’ (at paragraph [126]), even if resulting in a fine that could be described as
‘punitive’, did not establish the kind of severity that might bring the proceedings into the criminal sphere.

21 [2001] EWCA Civ 1014, [2001] 1 WLR 2253, at paragraph 67. LJ Potter gave the substantive opinion of the
majority and in which Mance LJ (as he then was) concurred. The dissenting opinion of Sir Martin Nourse did
not refer to Brown.

22 Application no 5556/10, 14 February 2019. See paragraphs 68 to 72.

23 The Commissioners for Revenue and Customs v Connaught Corporate Solutions Ltd, F-tT, TC/2017/05527,
dated 5 November 2018. See paragraphs 52 to 59.

24 At paragraph [68].

14
category of proceedings characterised as involving the determination of a criminal
charge (regardless of their characterisation under national law) was not closed.

32. The Tribunal stressed it had formed no view on the preliminary issue, but wished to be
addressed on the nature and role of the FRC and on the nature of proceedings by the
Tribunal to hear formal complaints in order to form a view as to whether those
proceedings involved the ‘determination of a criminal charge’ as that is understood in
the jurisprudence on Article 6 of the ECHR.

(ii)Case management directions relative to the preliminary issue
33. Mr Potts undertook to produce a short note, setting out the FRC’s position, which he
promptly provided in the early afternoon of the 12 May (this is referred to in paragraph
(d) of the directions issued later on 12 May, quoted below, as the FRC’s ‘outline
submission’). Having received that note, the Tribunal issued the following directions25:

‘The Tribunal is mindful that [the Respondent] is unrepresented but nonetheless
strongly encourage him to attend the hearing tomorrow, 13 May 2025, which will
commence at 11:00 to afford time for Mr Bowerman to travel to the International
Dispute Resolution Centre (‘the IDRC’, details of which were provided in a prior
email from [the Secretary]). The Tribunal will facilitate Mr Bowerman’s
participation at tomorrow’s hearing by:
a) commencing the hearing at 11:00 am,
b) having the Tribunal’s consideration of any entitlement to assistance with
legal representation considered as a preliminary issue,
c) providing him with its outline of that issue (see below),
d) providing him with the FRC’s outline submission on the preliminary issue;
e) providing him with copies of any cases relied upon;
f) requiring Counsel for the FRC to go take the Tribunal to the specific
paragraphs relied on in any cases cited, and
g) ensuring throughout the hearing that Mr Bowerman understands the
import of the issues being discussed.

Hard copies of the cases will be emailed with this Note, and hard copies will also
be available for Mr Bowerman at the IDRC tomorrow, as well.

Preliminary issue

The Tribunal notes Mr Bowerman’s reference to a desire to instruct legal
representation and his statement that he is without a means to pay for the same,
communicated by email on 6th May 2025.

25 Emailed to parties, including the Respondent, at 12:46 pm.

15
The Tribunal wishes to be addressed on a preliminary issue as whether these
proceedings involve the ‘determination of a criminal charge’ as that phrase is
understood in the jurisprudence on the right to a fair trial for the purposes of
Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (‘the EHCR’). If so, the
terms of Article 6(3) of the ECHR fall to be considered.

The Tribunal notes, in particular, the terms of Article 6(3)(a) providing for those
facing criminal charges (understood in a Convention sense, and in which the
domestic characterisation is not determinative) to defend himself or through legal
assistance or, if he does not have sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to
be afforded this for free when the interests of justice so require.

The Tribunal notes passages from the following two cases, which consider this
issue, and invite parties’ submissions on these.

1) The Commissioners for HMRC v Connaught Corporation Solutions
Limited26, First -Tier Tax Tribunal (FTT), Appeal No. TC/2017/05527,
dated 5 November 2018, at paras 48 to 60; and
2) SA-Capital OY v Finland, (application no 5556/10)27, dated 14 February
2019, European Court of Human Rights (First Section), at paras 65-75.

Evidence of means

We note that Mr Bowerman asserts that he has insufficient means to fund legal
representation. Mr Bowerman is strongly encouraged to evidence his means
(income, outgoings and assets) at the hearing tomorrow, 13 May 2025.

Even if Mr Bowerman is not able to provide this information in full to the
Tribunal tomorrow, he is strongly encouraged, and expected, to attend the
hearing tomorrow (13th May 2025 at the IDRC).’

A copy of the FRC’s outline submission the preliminary issue and the cases relied upon
were also provided to the Respondent by email.

26 The case of Connaught Corporation Solutions Limited was selected as it contained a recent, clear and
accessible summary of the case law addressing this issue.

27 SA-Capital OY v Finland (ECtHR First Section, Application no.5556/10, 14 February 2019):
https://hudoc.echr.coe.int/eng#{%22itemid%22:[%22001-189791%22]}.

16
Hearing on the preliminary issue on the morning of 13 May
34. The Tribunal reconvened on 13 May at 11:00 am. There was no appearance by the
Respondent. The Respondent had made no other communication after his email
(referring to an ‘appointment reminder with Adult Physiotherapy’) the previous day28.
He supplied no further information in respect of his non-attendance, nor in respect of
his financial means. He made no application to the Tribunal under paragraph 17 of the
Scheme or otherwise.

35. The Tribunal proceeded in his absence to consider the preliminary issue and heard Mr
Potts on that issue. It should be noted that neither Article 6(3)(c) of the ECHR nor
paragraph 17(ii) of the Scheme are expressed in absolute terms. The recipient must
demonstrate financial need (respectively, ‘has not sufficient means to pay for legal
assistance’ or ‘they cannot afford (and does not have adequate insurance cover for)
legal representation’). For the purposes of the discussion of the preliminary issue, Mr
Potts was asked to proceed on the hypothesis that that financial criterion had been
satisfied. Were any application to be made, the Respondent would also require to
satisfy paragraph 17(ii) of the Scheme.

The FRC’s submissions on the preliminary issue
36. In contending that the hearing of the Formal Complaint by the Tribunal did not involve
the determination of a criminal charge, Mr Potts referred to the following:

1) The case of R (Kuzmin) v General Medical Council29 to establish that the
conduct of professional disciplinary proceedings did not involve a determination
of a criminal charge. The court in that case had reviewed English and ECtHR
authorities, and concluded:

“34. Disciplinary tribunals are part of the regulatory scheme which governs the
relationship between professional associations and individuals who practise
that profession and, as a condition of doing so, sign up to that scheme. In form
they may have “charges” in the form of alleged breaches of the regulatory
scheme under which the individual operates, which are “prosecuted” by the
relevant regulatory authority; and, of course, disciplinary tribunals have the

28 Quoted above, at paragraph [26].
29 [2019] EWHC 2129 (Admin), [2019] 1 W.L.R. 6660 at [34]-[38], (Divisional Court, per Hickinbottom LJ).

17
power to impose sanctions for breaches which may have very severe
consequences for the individual involved. However, as the courts have
repeatedly emphasised, disciplinary proceedings are civil and not criminal
proceedings.”

2) The present proceedings, being a hearing on a formal complaint, were
professional disciplinary proceedings. This was apparent from:
a. Para (1) of the Scheme, which states its purposes as follows:

‘To protect the public, maintain public confidence in the accountancy
profession and uphold proper standards of conduct, this Scheme
provides a system for:-
(i)
the investigation of Members’… conduct in the course of
their professional activities… or otherwise, including such
conduct before they became Members… and
(ii)
if warranted following such investigation, bringing
disciplinary proceedings against Members....’; and

b. The document entitled ‘FRC’s Roles and Responsibilities: Schedule of
Functions and Powers’30. This described one of the FRC’s functions as
‘[p]roviding an independent investigation and discipline scheme for
matters relating to accountancy firms or members of the accountancy
professional bodies which raise or appear to raise important issues
affecting the public interest’. The corresponding enabling powers to
carry out this function had been conferred by ‘private arrangement with
CCAB Member Bodies, and CIMA’ on the FRC to provide ‘independent
investigation and/or disciplinary hearings in respect of misconduct by
accountant members/ member firms in public interest cases’31.

Mr Potts confirmed that there was no statutory underpinning for the foregoing
arrangement. It was a private, contractual scheme between the FRC and participating
accountancy professional bodies in which they, in effect, cede part of their disciplinary
functions to the FRC in cases involving important issues of public interest. So far as Mr
Potts was aware, this arrangement was unique. Accordingly, the FRC has jurisdiction,
in cases specified in paragraph 1(3) of the Scheme, to pursue disciplinary proceedings

30https://media.frc.org.uk/documents/FRC_Roles_and_Responsibilities_Schedule_of_Functions_and_Powers.pd
f . Hereinafter referred to as the ‘FRC’s Statement of Functions and Powers’.

31 See the unnumbered paragraph on page 10, under the heading ‘Corporate Report-Accounting’.

18
which could otherwise be pursued by the relevant Participant accountancy body. Whilst
the FRC has other, statutory functions (for present purposes this includes in relation to
audit), the investigation and discipline of accountancy members is not a statutory
function. Nor is it a function involving the exercise of state power in pursuit of wider
regulatory objectives, such as promoting competition by deterring or punishing price-
fixing cartels.32 He set out the FRC’s position that it did not accept that other
proceedings brought by it (whether pursuant to its statutory or non-statutory functions)
involve the determination of “criminal charges”. (That issue does not arise in these
proceedings and the Tribunal expresses no view on the characterisation for the purposes
of Art. 6 of the ECHR of other proceedings that may be brought by the FRC.)

37. Accordingly, in Mr Potts’ submission, the present proceedings involve the regulation of
the professional conduct of an individual member: in this case, specifically the
relationship of that member with the FRC as their regulator, and their duty to cooperate.
The Formal Complaint does not involve any allegation of criminal misconduct or
conduct akin to criminal behaviour. The FRC does not have powers to bring criminal or
quasi-criminal prosecutions (unlike some regulators such as the Financial Conduct
Authority which has criminal and civil enforcement powers). Moreover, the civil
standard of proof is applicable to these proceedings33.

38. In respect of the observation in SA-Capital OY of a ‘gradual broadening of the scope of
the criminal limb of Article 6 to cases not strictly belonging to the traditional
categories of criminal law34, Mr Potts submitted that there were limits to this
expansion. The category had never been extended to include professional disciplinary
cases. The three-fold Engel test, as for example applied in Han, remained the
appropriate way to ascertain whether or not proceedings involved the determination of
a criminal charge.

39. Mr Pott’s submission on the application of the three-fold Engel test was as follows:

32 cf SA-Capital OY v Finland (ECtHR First Section, Application no.5556/10, 14 February 2019):
https://hudoc.echr.coe.int/eng#{%22itemid%22:[%22001-189791%22]}.

33 See paragraph 12 of the Scheme.

34 SA-Capital OY v Finland, at [68].

19
1) How is the charge classified under domestic law?
The Formal Complaint was classified as civil under domestic law (albeit he
accepted that this was not determinative).

2) What is the substantive nature of the conduct in question?
Mr Potts cited Potter LJ (in Han at [66]):

109. From the cases noted, in the Tribunal’s view, there are several important and
intersecting public interests. As noted in Sharma, there is a public expectation that
regulators (and by which term we include disciplinary and other bodies charged with
oversight of the conduct of professionals) will investigate allegations of misconduct by
persons subject to that oversight. In the absence of an obligation on the part of the
professional person subject to those allegations to cooperate, those investigations may
be frustrated. That is detrimental in significant respects: it undermines the ability of the
relevant regulator (or professional body) to exercise effective oversight; at an individual

who has brought that complaint. It may also, as the Court in Robson (2002) observed,
bring the profession concerned into disrepute. Those are each in themselves serious
matters, but more serious still is the wider impact this may have in undermining public
confidence in both the profession and the regulatory process.

110. An individual who has obtained a professional certification, qualification or registration
is accorded a certain privileged status as a person whom members of the public may
trust to exercise their professional skills to the requisite standard and whom the public
may reasonably expect will be called to account if that standard is breached. It is for
that reason that, hard-won though that privilege may be, it brings obligations, including
an enduring obligation to submit to, and cooperate with, investigations by their
professional body. It is for these reasons that the Tribunal regards a failure to cooperate
with a regulator or disciplinary body as intrinsically serious.

111. On that analysis, the nature of the underlying conduct being investigated is not a
consideration to which we have had regard. Putting it another way, if a failure to
cooperate were treated as less serious because the underlying matters are characterised
as minor or even unproven, this may give rise to a perception that the obligation to
cooperate is mutable or its breach only a misdemeanour by virtue of that
characterisation. Such a perception could erode the obligation to cooperate and so
undermine the purpose of the Scheme. Further, if the nature of the underlying conduct
were more serious, this might encourage Members of the Scheme to take the view that
it is better to run the risk of a modest sanction for non-cooperation than to have the
underlying conduct exposed to investigation with the result of a potentially more
serious sanction. The recognition that a breach of the obligation to cooperate,
particularly if intentional, persistent, and without reasonable excuse, is itself a serious
matter and attracts a commensurately severe sanction will be dissuasive of that kind of
calculation.

The duty to co-operate with the Tribunal under paragraph 14 (1)

155. Paragraph 14 (1) of the Scheme says:

I read this to mean that a Member shall co-operate both with the EC and, separately,

having delivered the Formal Complaint to the Conduct Committee and the latter

with a notice (essentially, for non-attendance for interview) during an investigation.

first part of 14 (1)) during the investigation. This is reinforced by the fact that when the
Respondent committed breaches which resulted in the Formal Complaint, and so the
Allegations, he could not have owed a duty to a Tribunal because no Tribunal had been
appointed. The two are separate breaches and not one continuing breach avoiding the
problem of duplicity. Therefore, it is open to the Tribunal to sanction separately for the
second breach or, alternatively, to find that it should attract no separate sanction on some
higher principle such as, say, totality or fairness.

Intent

159. I am of the view that when deciding the appropriate sanction, it is only after a finding
of fact on the evidence that the Adverse Findings are made out, that the issue of
culpability is relevant (as are aggravating and mitigating factors). In my opinion, no
other sequence is logical because culpability can only be considered once the act or
omission has been proved through evidence. Paragraph 14 (1) simply places an
obligation that the Member “shall at all times co-operate fully” and does not address
degrees of culpability for a failure to not do so, this being dealt with - correctly in my
view - in the Sanctions Guidance. Where the Tribunal finds in its decision on merits, as
this Tribunal did, that the non-cooperation by the Respondent was ‘deliberate’, it is a
finding on culpability and not on whether the act, omission or conduct occurred. Such a
finding is highly relevant in the decision on sanction.

160. ‘Deliberate’ – a finding of this Tribunal when looking at the behaviour of the
Respondent - was to my mind used as an umbrella term. The Sanctions Guidance is
very helpful in that it distinguishes between two types of ‘deliberateness’: Intent and
Recklessness. The question to be answered is: Were the Respondent’s breaches of the
paragraph 14 obligations (and the duty owed to the Tribunal) simply recklessness on his
part or carried out with intent? The Guidance provides assistance in paragraphs 58 and
59.

161. Paragraphs 58 and 59 identify factors which tend to show whether the Misconduct (58)
or unspecified conduct (59) was either intentional or reckless. Key extracts relate to
whether the Member:
- ‘intended or foresaw that the likely…consequences of their actions or inactions would
amount to a falling short of professional standards of conduct (paragraph 58(a).
- ’permitted the Misconduct to continue notwithstanding that they knew that their actions
breached the relevant rules’ (paragraph 58(b).
- ‘repeated the Misconduct notwithstanding being aware that to do so would involve
breaching the relevant rules, standards or procedures’ (paragraph 58(f)).

- (a) knew that a proposed course of action or inaction might involve a breach of the
applicable professional standards, and (b) proceeded nevertheless.

This guidance identifies intent and recklessness as different degrees of culpability on the
Respondent’s part which, in my view, must be assessed in the alternative with full intent
attracting a higher sanction than mere recklessness.

That factors under the heading of intent are cited in the context of Misconduct does not
preclude them from being applied to other breaches such as those in issue here because
they are factors identified for illustrative purposes and, as such, not confined in their use.
I find them both helpful and relevant to the issue of sanction for the (two separate)
breaches identified here.

the formal Complaint (which addressed only non-cooperation with the EC and resulted

does not, in my view, eliminate the Tribunal’s discretion to reach a decision on

Tribunal. The Respondent was told what co-operation entailed, was reminded of the
consequences, and despite this decided not to cooperate, in different ways, at different

165. While agreeing with the sanction (in totality) proposed by colleagues, I arrive at the

Secondly, I am of the opinion that, as per paragraphs 66 and 67 of the Guidance,
deterrence must here be viewed as applicable in two distinct ways: deterring the

Sanction

166. In my opinion, the sanction should reflect the totality of Paragraph 14 breaches in the
Allegations but also the breach of the duty owed to the Tribunal. It should of course be

Starting, say, with a sanction of three years exclusion and increasing that to reflect

The Scheme and Sanctions Guidance

167. Paragraph 9(8)(ii) of the Scheme does not mandate and only invites consideration as to
whether the Tribunal should make an award of costs. It also confers a wide discretion to

168. Paragraph 75 of the Sanctions Guidance, on the other hand, refers only to a) “costs
incurred by the FRC” and b) that the Tribunal may “take account of the Member’s
financial position”. I interpret this to mean that, in order to be awarded, some evidence
that the costs were incurred by the FRC must be provided. Secondly, that the Tribunal
has the discretion as to whether to take account of the Member’s financial position. I
also note that this is guidance for the Tribunal and not a rule which must be strictly
followed.

169. There is no reference in the Scheme or Sanctions Guidance to other factors or
adjustments to be taken into account such as fairness or ensuring costs are reasonable
and proportionate to the case, which in commercial litigation provide a mechanism for
judicial control over legal costs.

The EC’s submissions

170. On 23 July 2025 the Tribunal received by email a document from the FRC’s Legal
services Team entitled ‘Schedule of Costs as at 18 July 2025’ for a total of £19,054.
These costs relate to Counsel (£16,298), FRC legal Assistant (£2,396) and
Disbursements (£360). There are two relevant points made in the Notes:

(i) An additional figure will be provided at the hearing for fees incurred after 18
July 2025, in preparing for and appearing at the resumed Tribunal hearing, and
(ii) this figure includes time spent on tasks partly or completely associated with the
investigation of the underlying allegations of Misconduct, rather than the failure
to co-operate. Arriving at a precise division between the two is not possible, due
to the way in which the time has been recorded.

The schedule and notes are significant for three reasons; firstly, because the Schedule
is acceptable evidence for me that the £19,054 was a cost incurred by the FRC up to
that date for investigating and hearing only the Formal Complaint; secondly, it makes
clear that Counsel’s fees for the resumed hearing were not included but would be
provided later, inferring that it anticipated incurring them for the resumed hearing and
would provide evidence, and; thirdly, that an attempt at adjustment had been made
(using estimation) to reduce the recorded costs which, it is implied, would otherwise
overstate the correct allocation for ‘time spent’ costs on investigating the Formal
Complaint and the Disciplinary Hearing arising from it.

171. Then on 23 July 2025, the Tribunal received by email a second document from the
FRC’s Legal services Team entitled ‘Tribunal Schedule of Costs as at 24 July 2025’
for a total of £37,459.79. The detailed breakdown confirms that all of these relate to the
Disciplinary Hearing, specifically Venue, Transcription, Convener, Tribunal attendance
and preparation and Expenses. The Notes state “+ TBC” against two items related to
Tribunal Members fees and expenses, presumably for items which had not been
incurred or claimed.

172. At the sanctions hearing on 24 July 2025, Mr Potts told the Tribunal, calculating on the
spot as he did so, that his fees for preparation for the resumed hearing required 3 hours

86
plus one day and that this would be £2,688 (including VAT). Various employees from
the FRC were present at the hearing but neither challenged nor explicitly confirmed that
the FRC deemed this to be incurred by it. Since then the FRC has confirmed by email
that these costs have been incurred.

The Respondent’s financial position

173. Paragraph 75 of the Sanctions Guidance allows the Tribunal discretion as to taking into
account the Respondent’s financial position when making an award of costs. Given that
the Tribunal is not bound to take this into account but may do so, the first decision
which must be made is whether the Tribunal wishes to exercise its discretion and take
into account at his financial position. No guidance is offered on how this is to be carried
out in terms of a list of factors to consider, or high-level regulatory principles, such as
is the case for sanction.

174. However, I considered the following factors in deciding the issue on the basis that
general principles of fairness and proportionality require me to do so:

1) In my view the Respondent chose not to attend the hearings. By doing so
he knowingly gave up the opportunity to put forward his case on costs,
including his financial position.
2) In the Hearing Bundle there is mention of the Respondent’s length of
employment in what was a senior financial position in a mid-size
international firm ([Company X]) for many years and that he also was
earning after leaving that firm. Moreover, we also learned that he was in
his mid-fifties in age. Even if the Tribunal has the discretion to draw
conclusions as to means from that, I would not. Neither of these are in any
practical way useful in establishing the Respondent’s financial position as
of today.
3) In an email on affordability and means on legal representation (not strictly
relevant on costs), the EC in an email made the point that to go beyond
mere assertion on means would require the Respondent to make a full
statement as to his income, assets and liabilities, and produce copies of all
documents necessary to substantiate the statement. The statement should

87
also provide details of any disposal of assets with a value in excess of
£250,000. The Tribunal could, using its discretion, have waived that high
evidential standard had the Respondent appeared before us, but he chose
not to attend the hearings and so forfeited the opportunity.

Taking account these factors that I would decline to exercise discretion to look at the
Respondent’s financial position.

Other Factors
175. I note that in civil actions in England & Wales, it is usual that costs follow the event –
the loser pays reasonable costs of his opponent. This is a ‘civil’ hearing resulting from a
contractual arrangement between Member and, ultimately, the FRC, and so my starting
position is that the Member should pay costs, subject to the Scheme rules and
Guidance. Also, that Regulatory objectives include deterring future misconduct by
ensuring that Members who commit breaches bear the financial burden of their actions.
The risk of having to pay regulatory costs from non-cooperation may encourage firms
or individuals to cooperate early and settle matters, reducing the need for lengthy
enforcement. I also note that other regulatory bodies such as the FCA and SRA can
recover costs in disciplinary cases where the respondent is found to be at fault, as is the
case here.

Award of Costs

176. Applying the relevant paragraphs of the Scheme and Sanctions Guidance, I find that the
costs in the two Schedules, £37,459.79 and £19,054, which makes a total of
£56,513.79, should be awarded in full as they are costs only in respect of the hearing of
the Formal Complaint and incurred by the FRC. They are payable to the FRC by the
Respondent within 28 days from the date of this award.

177. As to the additional amount calculated by Mr Potts in respect of his fees for the
resumed hearing on sanction of £2,688, I would add this sum given that formal
confirmation has now been received that this amount has been incurred by the FRC.
